articles.text:
WORKING MEN'S PLATFORM;

Nonnivo can be of greater importance to
the working class than that they should exercise
at the next election their newly-acquired voting
for members of Parliament in a manner which
shall command the respect of those to whom
they tire opposed. That the object which they
have in view shall be not only of benefit to
them as a class, but of advantage to the
nation; and I confidently submit to you that
an attempt to pay off the National Debt would
not only benefit them as a alas's, but be of the
greatest advantage to the nation.

Taxes would then be taken off to the extent
of nearly £30,000,000 (£28,198,928,) and the
working class would then cheerfully return
to their daily toil without having paid an
tax for any article which they consumed at
breakfast or the tobacco which imparts com-
fort to him, and this would enable him to
compete in the markets of the world with the
Germans, who, like themselves, would not
have to pay the interest of any National
Debt.

As no one will gainsay the great advantage
the nation would receive by the payment Of
the National Debt, mynext step waste showhow
this could be done, and had the Commissionete
of her Majesty's -Inland Revenue performed
their duty, and made a return which the
House of Commons ordered upon the motion
of a friend of mine, I could have shown you
with more distinctness than I am now able
to do.

The Report of the Commissioners of her
Ilsjesty's Inland Revenue," is a document
perfectly disgraceful to a civilized country.
In the first place it carries a lie upon its feat
and for an account to have so damning
a blot
vitiates its whole character; no advantage nen
possibly be reaped from such a document
which occupies the attention of many elerlr6'
and costs a considerable sum of money 1010
15 just so much money thrown a*tay.

The Report of the Commissioners now
purports to be a report of the Inland Revenue
for tho. years ended 25th March, 1870 and
1871, yet in page 42 the report says in the
year 1869-70 each penny produced 1,499,331;
we are not yet able to give the result for 1870-
71, but may reasonably expect that it will
show considerable increase over 1869-70; but
" if the Commissioners are not yet able to give
the result for 1870.71," why, in the name of
common honesty, do they endorse their re-
ports with these words—"for the years ended
31st March, 1870 and 1871 ? "
This enables the sub. who has management
of the work, in this instance, I believe Mr. W.
H. ar4DSTONE, to postpone at his pleasure,
and, indeed, entirely to burke the order of
the House of Commons which required it;
and, cf course, these parties always have a
falsehood at their fingers' ends to excuse
such conduct. Mr. GLAnsroNE knew that
his father was against paying off the National
Debt, and therefore his son postpones obey-
ing an order of the House of Commons •for
a return which would have shown clearly
the ease by which the National Debt might
be paid off.
There is also another very important
element which should induce the working
class to adopt this platform, and which con -
sista in the fact that during the recess Earl
DEtory. went twice out of his way to im-
press on the minds of those who heard him
the expediency of paying off the National
Debt. Mr. DIRIAELI also brought under
the attention of the House the important
fact that he had introduced the plan of in-
vesting all surplus revenue into terminable
annuities, so that they could not be seized
by a rapacious Chancellor of the Exchequer.
But although , Mr. GransroNE's delay in
making the returns has prevented my bring-
ing under your attention the figures in de-
tail, yet the report of the Commissioners
proves that the national income is more than
16 times the interest on the debt; in other
words, the nation is in precisely the same
position as an individual would be who had
to pay interest to the amount of only £26
per annum out of an income of £430, leav-
ing himself a clear income of above £406 per
annum.

RIGBY WASON.

articles.title: GREAT ESSENTIAL.
articles.text:
THE GREAT ESSENTIAL.

BELIEVING ignorance to be the source of
most of the social and political evils that afflict
society, I regard educational knowledge to be
the great essential, the grand panacea, of our
social and political salvation.
With these views thousands concur, and yet
we meke but slow progress with the real educa-
tion of our people. Is not this to be attributed
o the erroneeue notions that prevail regarding
kin 4 of education, or the great essentials
of knowledge that ought to be given to our
youthful population.
Instead of regarding the being to be educated
as one of our future brother -sisters, on
whose properly developed mental and moral
pi:mere or shortcomings, will depend not only
his or her own happiness or misery, but also
that of others they will be surrounded by;
instead of this, many are too often disposed to.
regard the individual from their own petty
point qf view; and to seek to mould him in
thP s4tereste ef their own sect or party; to
make hint:a mere useful drudge or tool, or to
regard him Ens an inferior being, for whom the
smallest modicum of education is sufficient,
such as a little reading, writing, and cipher-
ing, and then to cast him forth to tight the
great battle of life without knowledge or prin-
ciples to direct or guide him, and • to let him
blunder on as he best may.
Far too many among us 'are apt to think
that if a child has received a little reading,
writing, and ciphering he is fully equipped for
the voyage of life; they believing that he has
then the instruments for acquiring knowledge
for himself, such persons failing to perceive
that the motive power is wanting to urge him
on, which is some amount of elementary know-
ledge to appreciate the necessity for acquiring
more. Not only this, but the mind un-
quickened by knowledge is less
.disposed to
seek and acquire, amid the strife and conten-
tions of life, than it is when the mind is Touni

and plastic and anxious to acquire, if the
knowledge is properly laid before it.
Those, however, who entertain such narrow
views of education would do well to read the
observations lately put forth on this important
point by Sir JOIIN LUBBOCK. He very ably
and truly said that " a child is not educated
when he can read, write, and cipher ; " that
"reading and writing no more make education
than a knife and fork make a dinner," and he
very earnestly proposes that we shall not only
give the children the knife and fork, but
intellectual food as well. Of the kinds of
intellectual food, he says that among other
things, encouragement ought to be given to the
teaching of history, geography, elementary
social economy, &e. In fact, he wishes
children to possess some knowledge of the
world they live in; some information regard-
ing the life and doings of our forefathers, and
the many struggles society has made to advance
from barbarism to our present state of civiliza-
tion; and some knowledge to direct and
guide them in the pursuit of that which is
necessary to their social and political well-
being.
Regarding this last kind of knowledge—
elementary social science—as all-important to
be given in our schools, I wish here to
introduce to the readers of the BEE-HIVE a
meritorious effort that has lately been made
to simplify to the capacity of children this
kind of knowledge. It is put forth in a little
work, entitled "Helps to the Young, in their
Efforts at Self-Guidance." It is edited by the
Rev. W. JOWITT, Head Master of the Middle
Class Schools, in Cowper-street; and though
it is especially addressed to the young, it is
meant to aid the teacher in imparting to his
pupils lessons on social life, and human well-
being. It is a work, too, that our working
classes should read, and, in fact, has a special
claim to the attention of all truly interested in
the education of our people. In justice to
others, however, I am bound to state that
ninny other efforts have previously been made
to simplify the elements of social Science, such
as arc set forth in " Lesons on the Phenomena
of industrial Life," edited by the Dean of
HEnEFonD ; "Outlines of Social Economy,
and Progressive Lessons on Social 53ie50e," by
Mr. Ews ; " Easy Lessons on Money
Matters," by Archbishop WILITELY, and several
others.

ENCLOSURE OF COMMONS AND
WASTE LANDS.

PIII3LIC attention ought at once to be called
to the fact that a Bill is now before the House
of Lords for the enclosure and appropriation,
in some form or other unknown to the public,
of considerable portions of commonable land.
Sir T. SINCLAIII inquired of the PRIMER, a
few nights ago, "whether hii attention had
been directed to the roportof the Inclosure
Commissioners for this Year, in which it Was
stated, that upwards of eight millions of
acres of common and commonable land stili
remained inclosed and waste, or about one.-
Utli of the soil of England, or equal to ton
average counties; that at the rate of the pro-
gress for the last:twenty-five years, it would
take upwards of a century before one-third of
this area is dealt with; that three millions of
acres of this land is to be found in the low-
land counties; that at least one million of
these acres might be added to the productive
area of agricultural land, being More than the
Dutch have now won from the sea in three
and a-half centuries, and one-tenth of all the
land under crop in England, exclusive of

grass.' "
Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to Sir T. SIN-
CLAIR, said, "That the government had been
aware that it is extremely desirableihat there
should be some legislation on the subject of
enclosures, and that the useful applica-
tion of labour, as a means of increasing
the supply of agricultural products, should
not be retarded for any length of time. A
Bill had already been introduced into the
other House dealing with the subject, and
would shortly be in the hands of members of
this lieuse." Now, it is to be hoped that the
Land Tenure Reform. Associations, and snch
members of Parliament as really have ally de.
desire to preserve the 0001IROU lands of this cowl.

,

try to their rightful owners, namely, the people,
will enter their solemn protest against a single
acre of these lands being sold or otherwise
disposed of than being cultivated, and let to
suitable tenants, the rents being paid into the
public Exchequer, to form a portion of the
general revenue of the country. If this were
done, co-operative farming might be carried
out with complete success, and with great
advantage, both to those occupying this land,
and the country at large. But if these lands
are to be sold, the purchase-money will be
fritted away in a manner that will in no way
benefit the country, and another gigantic
robbery and absorption of the common lands of
this country will have been perpetrated upon
the people. All that is required is that
Parliament should authorise these common
lands to be put into tolerable condition, and
then let them in small or moderate sized
farms, to be formed either on th% 00-operative
principle, or by individuals, whichever may
be found to answer best. Now, it may be
urged that by selling these common lands,
Parliament will get rid of all further re-
sponsibility, besides obtaining the ready
cash.

With regard to future responsibility, both
Parliament and Government can very easily
be relieved of this by the appointment or
election of local overseers by the ratepayers in
the counties where these common lands are
situate, who would be accountable for the
payment of rents they received the same as
any other inland revenue officer, and that is
all either Government or Parliament ought to
have to do in the matter, except the right
to inquire if such lands were properly managed.
Now, we hear a great deal from time to
time about the reduction of taxation, and we
have the Financial Reform Association, and
the Anti-Income Tax Association, and at
election times Liberals and Conservatives vie
with each other in their professions for
lightening the burdens of the people; bu
have any of the leaders of these associations,
or pseudo - retrenching politicians ever
calculated the immense amount of revenue
that would be produced, and an equal amount
saved to the country in taxes, by putting a
considerable portion of the best parts of our
common lands into tenantable condition, and
the revennee derived therefrom, paid into the
public exchequer, instead of going into the
pockets of private individuals P Here is where
the land may be made to yield a portion of the
public revenue which would greatly lighten
other descriptions of taxation.
All those at all acquainted with the tenure
and conditions upon which land was held in
the early periods of the history of this country
know that the entire revenue of the nation was
derived from land; and without entering at
present into the question of how far we ought
to restore that ancient practice, we ought, at,
least, to avail ourselves of the revenues that
may be derived from the letting of the best
portions of our common and waste lands
instead of selling them to capitalists, the
proceeds of which would never be of any sen-
sible benefit to the nation.

Moreover, this would form an excellent
opportunity for enabling the most fitting
portion of the agricultural labourers to be
placed upon the land and have a direct
interest in its cultivation, as we may rest
assured that something in this way will have
to be done before long. The agitation now
going on in the agricultural districts is of
greater import, and means a vast deal more in
the end than the more raising of their wages a
shillings per week. The time is fast approach-
ing when these men will insist upon having a
direct interest in the occupancy and cultiva-
tion of the land, and it would be an act of
wisdom upon the part of those who have tbe
power, to put the best portions of our waste
and common lands into a tenantable condition
and let them out in farms to the most
suitable and deserving of the agricul-
tural population, either to be worked
upon the principle of co-operative farming, or
by their own individual exertions. Such a
course of action as this 'mild not fail to
increase considerably the agricultural produce
of the -nation, and, give the °couriers of
those holding a dittet interest In the cultiva-
tion of land, by being directly attioilefi to it,.

and at the same time be a fruitful sourbe.of
revenue, and enable the CHANCELLOR of the
EXCHEQUER to make a corresponding reduc-
tion of taxation.

But if these lands arb to be sold aad pass
for ever from the public, a grave responsibility
will rest with those who would thus he guilty of
betraying the public interest in these landg,
and it is the duty of Parliament to prevent the
passing of any Act which might take away from
the people of this country their right to retain
possess'on of the common and waste lands within
the United Kingdom. I have been waiting
aftxiously for the last fortnight, fullyexpeeting
the Land Tenure Reform Association, or some
other influential persons, drawing the attention
of the country to the Bill now before the
House of Lords for dealing with the common
lands and protesting against their being taken
from the people. But as no action appears
yet to have been taken by anyone, I, at least,
enter my humble, but solemn and determined
protest against a single inch of the common
public, lands of this country being sold and
filched from the people.

INTRODUCTION.

No prospect of an immediate settlement of
this dispute is at present apparent; and it is
very probable the strike on the part of the
joiners will exist for several weeks longer, It
may not be out of place here to define its
exact position at the present time. Up to the
lock, out on the 17th of June, the only two
branches of the building trade who had pre-
sented memorials to the employers for "the
nine hours and 9d. per hour," were the masons
and the joiners. The strike of the latter
against two large firms belonging to the
Masters' Association produced the lock-out,
throwing out of employment the men in the
other branches who had taken no part in the
movement— the painters, plasterers, brick-
layers, metal-workers, and labourers. In self-
defence these branches at once p.oceeded to
organize committees, to collect funds to support
the number locked out, and an amalgamated
committee was formed, composed of rwo
delegates from the committee of each trade.
Before, however, this organization was com-
pleted, the lock-out was withdrawn by the
masons coming to an arrangement with the
masters. 'The masons at once withdrew tram
the amalgamated committee, and the com-
mittees of the other branches, with the ex-
ception of the joiners, having reviewed their
position, and. finding that their organization
and pecuniary resources did not warrant them

it appears that the employers generally are

following letter from the Amalgamated Buildere'

Wilito Rose Tavern. Castle-street, Leicester-

.Sir,—l hate to aeknost ledge the receipt of your

scarcely apply to our cotninittee, because at the time

- -
2, Westminster Chambers, July 22, 1872.
Sir —Your letter of the 20th inst. was laid
before the committee of the Central Association of
Master Builders this day, and I am requested to
say in reply that the terms on which the shops
and works in London !lave been re-opened allow
a reduction of the hours of labour to an

presented by them. Beyond these concessions the
master builders are on no account prepared to go,

The above letter virtually rescinds the masters'

THE AMALGAMATED COMMITTEE.
A meeting of the amalgamated trades com-
mittee was hold on Tuesday afternoon, at the
White Rose Tavern, Castle-street,Leicester-square.
There was in attendance Messrs. Coulson and
Batchelor, for the bricklayers; Messrs. Sainebury
and Westaby for the plasterers ; Messrs. Sinclair
and Barry for the carpenters; Mr. Kenny for the
labourers ; Messrs. Shipton arid Watkins for the
painters; and Messrs. Leverett and Vivian for
the metal workers.
Mr. Shipton, the secretary, read the letter he
had received from Mr. Bird, and considerable
discussion followed.
A resolution was adopted authorising the Secre-
tary to reply in diplomatic style. merely disclosing
the general ground which the trades wish to as.
mune in future negotiation. In the last letter he
had pointed out, as two objectionable features in

for the fundamental principle of the nine hours,
and the omission of any safeguard against having

terms to other trades. The committee wish to
make out the best ease they can againt the masons'
arrangement of hours, especially in the winter.
In the rear of that the code of working rules will
be brought into play. There is here a substantial
acceptance of the interview offered, but it is only
provisional. As soon as the amalgamated com-
mittee has arranged for terms, they must refer to
their constituents for autherity to treat practically.
It hopes that the masters' central committee will
grant a preliminary interview at which a platform
may be framed with a view to the separate trades
taking the opinion of their members upon it. The
phase into which the strike is entering now will
therefore be circumlocutory as well as indefinite
and partial. The carpenters virtually hold aloof
from the proceeding, though nominally they are
one of the negotiating parties. The basis of a
compromise has first to be framed between the
masters' central committee and the Amalgamated
Trades Committee; then it has to he voted upon
by a host of societies and shops before there can
be any specific discussion of terms.
The committee then proceeded with the ar
rangement of the details for the llyde-park
nv,eting on this evening (Saturday). It is under-
stood that the carpenters are not to take any part
, in the meeting.

branch.

MEETING OP POSTMEN.

A. meeting of letter-carriers attached to the
Chief Office, London, E.C., on Monday morn-
ing in their kitchen, to appoint two delegates to
represent them on the Committee of London Post-
oftioe employs now being formed in order to wait
upon the Postmaster-General, to place before him
the inadequacy of the pay they receive to meet
the increase in the price of nearly all articles of
necessity which has been going on for several
years past, but which has assumed such serious
proportions during the last few months. The
meeting was to have been held on Saturday, but
was forbidlen by the Superintendent until the
consent of the Postmaster had been obtained, at
the same time informing them that he would at
once convey any request to that effect. Applica-
tion was at once made to the postmaster of the
Rat Central district for permission to hold the
meeting, which was at once granted, those apply-
ing being informed they would be held respon-
sible for any violent language that might be used.
The chairman opened the meeting by a few
judicious remarks, saying that if any persons
present misconducted themselves in any way by
word or deed, so as to give a just cause of offence
to the authorities, he would immediately vacate
the chair. Ile urged upon all present the necessity
of united action, but to keep themselves within
the bounds of prudence, and on no account to act
contrary to the rules and regulations of the service.
The following resolution was proposed by Mr.
Ilattam, letter carrier, and seconded by Mr.
Kebble, letter carrier, and carried unanimously :
That this meeting of the East Central letter
carriers, finding their present rate of pay in-
sufficient for the necessities of themselves and
families, and considering the revised scale no
improvement thereon, do hereby appoint two
of their number to represent them, to act
upon and in unison with the Postal Employees
Committee (now forming), with the object of
waiting upon the Postmaster-General, and desire
them to inform that gentleman that nothing loss
than granting the whole asked for in their petition
of Marsh last can possibly be considered as a final
settlement of the question, and also pledges itself
i
to support them n their efforts to obtain it; and
they at the same time desire to express their deep
and earnest sympathy with their brethren in the
suburbs and provinces who are now moving in the
same direction, and trust that their ellbrts will be
attended with the success they undoubtedly merit.
In aocordance with the above resolution, the
following delegates were unanimously chosen,
viz.:—Mr. William Booth, proposed by Mr.
Wright, letter carrier, and seconded by Mr. Rad-
ford, letter carrier; and Mr. William Sirett, pro-
posed by Mr. Mogridge and seconded by Mr. 11.
Dalley. An amendment which was, proposed fell
through. A vote of thanks was then passed to the
postmaster for his courtesy in so kindly granting
the use of the kitchen.

The first meeting of delegates on the Postal
Employes' Deputation was held on Tuesday, the
23rd inst. 'I wenty-four gentlemen were present,
representing the Registered letter, Foreign, Inland,
Newspaper, East Central, and District Offices.

Meetings are taking or are about to take place
for the election of delegates for departments not
yet represented.

TUE POSTAL EMPLOYES' DEPUTATION.

It is our duty, in this the hour of action, to en-
courage the delegates who are about to meet the Post-
master-General. The cause they have to represent
is a just one, and there is no reason to fear. They
mitist remember that however they may be biassed
by their own feelings, that it will be necessary to
consult their fellows before they accept anything
as a final settlement. Be firm, temperate, and
respectful, ye delegates, and show to your broth°
officers that their choice has not been misplaced.r
In the first place, they must agree upon the plan
of action, and firmly adhere to it, and in the
Argument alwayi be general, as the authorities

always try to make these interviews personal.
The men are all willing and ready to back you up,
and we hope that your efforts will be crowned
with success. After agreeing upon what shall be
asked for, they must write to the Postmaster-
General acquainting him with the fact of a deputa-
tion being about to wait on him, and ask him to
appoint a day which la in be convenient to receive
them; those who have the power are both able and
willing to support you if you require it. Our
earnest hopes are that this course will be sufficient
without having resort to stronger measures. It
is a great pity that the superintending officers
in these hard times among the men should
be so ill-advised as to annoy any man
who is considered "dangerous ;" they should
rather try and Conciliate them, and perhaps might
be able to servo their chiefs and their country by
so doing; instead of which, they act so as to raise
the bitterest feelings of the men, To the sorters,
sub-sorters, and letter-carriers, our advice is that,
pending the meeting between the delegates and
the Postmaster-General, that they should so con-
duct themselves that the severest martinet cannot
accuse them of any dereliction of dut3 , and they
should so strengthen the hands of their represen-
tatives by means of money, and by showing a
bold front, as to make their cause sure of success.
It is of no use for men to grumble unless they are
prepared to support those who endeavour to remove
the cause of complaint, an it is hoped that now
the delegates are appointed that they will quit
themselves like men, and try and not allow their
feelings of unjust treatment to make them disre-
spectful to their superintending officers.

THE LONDON MAT AND MATTING

WEAVERS.

At a meeting of the London Trades Council,
held on Wednesday evening at the Bell Inn, Old
Bailey, Mr. E. Coulson in the chair, Messrs.
Green and Adams attended as a deputation from
the Mat and Matting Weavers' Society, to lay the
case of their trade before the council. ;From
statements made by the deputation, it appeared
that a few years since the average wages of the
operatives in the trade had been per week, but
that for some time past the average was only 225.
per week. This great reduction in wages had
arisen front the extensive manufacture of mats
and matting in the convict prisons throughout the
kingdom. For the bast ton years the operatives
have been endeavouring to induce the Govern-
ment to employ the convicts in various trades in
fair proportions, instead of employing them in
one special trade, and thus, by a severe and
unnatural competition, reducing the wages of the
honest workmen in that trade to so low a scale as
to render it impossible for them properly to main-
tain themselves and families. They had recently
solicited the employers to rearrange the smile of
prices for work, which would have increased the
wages by about 33. per week, making them 4s. 2(1.
per day, for 101 hours' work. The employers
having refused this request, the operatives had
ceased working, and they now asked the council to
give them a certificate enabling them to appe 11 to
the trades societies generally for suppoit. They
also requested the council to appoint a deputation
to the Home Secretary to point out the evils of
employing convicts almost exclusively in one
trade. After some discussion it was resolved to
grant the certificate as requested, but that the
question of a deputation stands over for further
consideration. The council then proceeded to
transact its ordinary business, in which there was
nothing of general interest. The Boiler-makers
and Iron Shipbuilders' Society joined the council
last evening..

A second large meeting of farmers and dealers
and others connected with the agricultural in-
terest was held in the spacious Corn Exchange,
Oxford, after the business of the market on
Saturday afternoon, to promote the association
being formed for protecting the interests of the
employers of agricultural labour. This action has
been considered necessary in consequence of the
attempt to force upon the employers the rules of
the "National Labourers' Union."

Mr. Westover, of Donator, occupied the chair,
and it was unanimously resolved that the Associa-
tion should be designated "The Oxfordshire
and Adjoining Counties Association of Agri..
culturists." Among (ther rules it was agreed
that no member should employ a labourer
belonging to a Union unless he is already a hired
servant, and that the Association should take
legal proceedings, if necessary, to protect the
servants of its members against intimidation or
annoyance. Branch associations will be imam.
diately formed in various parts of the county. A

SATURDAY, JULY 27, 1872.

TIIE LONDON JOINERS' STRIKE.

As yet the matters in dispute between the
carpenters and joiners and the employers in
the building trades remain unsettled; and, what
is worse, we are not aware that any serious,
well-considered attempt has been recently
made from either side to settle them, The
fencing, by way of correspondence, so far, has
lacked that thoughtfulness which the gravity
of the ease demands. An imaginary "point
of honour" has been set up by each Committee,
and they keep floating about these in a pur-
poseless sort of way, which can have no effect
but to stupidly prolong a struggle in the
immediate termination of which both are
strongly interested. The real, and the only
real " point of honour "in this case is, that
which will secure in the speediest way the
most equitable settlement. There is no other
—there can be no other. Anything else is
mere delusion, which sensible men ought to
see through, and drive out from amongst
them.

When we first undertook to express an
opinion on this dispute we pressed on the
men to re-open the question with a view to
arbitration. We press this upon their con-
sideration again. We asked them not to
withdraw an atom of their case from the
jurisdiction of the arbitrators, and we repeat
now that this is their only true policy. It
the employers consented to-morrow to arbitrate
on the one, instead of on the three questions

in dispute, it would he wisdom on the part
of the men to put in the other two and ask
for a settlement by deliberation and reason
over every inch of the disputed ground. We
tell them that the principle of arbitration is in-
valuable to working men. It is all powerful
for the furtherance of their interests, not
simply as a power to advance with during
seasons of exceptional briskness of trade,
but as a power to resist the attacks of the
employers in times of exceptional sleekness.
In the past struggles of working men there
ought to have been ene ugh of suffering and
loss to convince them of this. And if, in
cases like the present, they will fight rather
than tit gotiate on equitable conditions, they
furnish melanchuly proof that experience has
come to them without profit, and, if purchased
at all, will have to be paii for at a rate pro-
portioned to the stupidity by which the tole
and fitting oppoitunity was missed.

What we apply here to the conduct of the
men is equally true of the en plo/ers, though
they have, to some extent, rectified their first
mistake. Their origintd blunder was serious,
their losses, by strikes aul lock-outs, me
heavy, and these, in many instances, are
attributable to a stupid determination on their

parts to carry things against their men
with a high hand, and in a spirit of
vulgar self-will which can only be excused by
the fact that many of them have become pros-
perous as employtrs, whose good sense aud
manliness have by no means kept pace with
the growth of their wealth.

The cultivation of a better feeling in both
paities—employers and employed—will have
its best chance of development when they
como together in a fiiendly spirit to settle
their difference and any impediment placed
in the way of this most desirable mutual

action, is a serious injury not ouly to the cause
of labour, but to all legitimate interests be-
longing to our national industry.

articles.text:
WORKSHOPS FOR SOLDIERS.

IN reply to Mr. iiAsnuirr Tit4CY, the other
evening, in the House of Commons, Mr. CARD-
WELL stated that measures had been taken for
instructing soldiers in carpentering, bricklay-
ing, and other trades, and regimental work-
shops had been established at. some stations.
At other plea s sites had been seltcted for the
erection of workshops. Qualified officers had
ban appointed to supervise the industrial
training of the men, and endeavours would be
made to utilize military labour in the repair
and erection of barracks.

This being the substance of what Mr.
CARDWELL uttered, we do not pretend to
know what sort of elaborate scheme it may be
the prelude to. There are many ways in
which such a general idea might be worked
out profitably; but on the other hand it might
be carried into effect in such a manner as to
be very detrimental to the interests of work.
lug men belonging to the trades about to be
taught in the training sehools of the army.
It is right that industry should be encouraged
rather than idleness amongst our soldiers. It
is not pleasant to think that large numbers of
able-bodied young men should be taken annually!
from the ranks of labour and trained in no-
thing but the art of destroying human life.
Hammers or trowels would better become the
handsof our young red-coated heroes than those
half.peuny switches which they flourish so
gracefully when they air themselves in the
cool of the afternoon. But before encourage-
ment be given to such a scheme as that spoken
of in Parliament, we should like to know what
it actually means. How it is to commence,
and in what direction, and with what intent
it is to be developed? There can be no objec-
tion to such au organization of industry in
the army as may meet certain requirements
of the service with as little cost as possible to
the tax-payers of the country. Bat with a
middle and upper class Parliament, and an
administration not p irticularly solicitous us to
the rights and requirements of working men,
it will be necessary to watch narrowt,y that
this new plan may not carry in it those dan-
gers to winking men's interests, indicated by the
way in which prison labour has been brought
into competition with free labour, to the ruin
of those who have to live honestly out of
prison. - The working men of England will
not, we are sure, stand in the way of any-
thing that may be dune usefully for the
uatiun in this direction, but they will not
submitto have their labour interfered with by
supplies which can be used to their injury,
either by ignorance or design on the part of
those who set them in motion. Every attempt
to organize labour by the Government should
be watched at every step of its progress. Up
to the present moment, all such attempts have
been unfavourable, rather than otherwise, to
the interests of our workers, and if such a
svitem is to go on, its intent must be above
su-picion, and its practice will have to find a
quite different direction from that which has
been given to it in certain of our public insti-
tutions. It would ba premature to suspect
that the Governm !nt 0 mid permit such
labour to be employed by contractors under
any circumstances, but it may be as well to
say in time, that any suJi net will be viewed
by the operatives of the country as a direct
and most flagrant attackon their rights and
interest, and will be resented as such.

articles.text:
GOVERNMENT.

A LIST has just been published af the
female prisoners and of the chiLlren ar-
, ested at the de of the recent struggle in
Paris. A more melancholy document it would
he diffieult to imagine. It is had enough when
strong men fling themselves into such struggles,
but with them sometimes it is an admitted
and paramount duty. To upset an authority
that devastste4 society in the name of law,
-hould not be shrunk from at the fitting op-
portunity, any more than the setting up in
the face of danger, of justice, and wisdom, ie
-the high places of power. But when women
and children show themselves in the front of
such a conflict, expose their lives, and sacrifice
them, for what they believe to be a righteous
cause, it should be taken as proof that the
very blood of life has been turned to gall, and
that the society whet° such things are pos-
sible, carries in its bosom evils utterly
incurable by ordinary social restoratives.

If we consider as true the assertion that
women and boys were drawn into the san-
guinary struggle in Paris by poverty, and the
Feneral demoralization of society, we make
matters no better. Why is society eter-
nally on the verge of these shocking
revolts? Why are men, women, and even
children prepared to descend into the streets
and join a carnival of bloodshed which is
altogether the result of rage and despair,
scarcely, if at all, animated by a heroic, high-
minded hope? Wny did ARTUUR YOUNG,
SMOLLET, and others tell us, before the first
great revolution broke out, that the sufferings
of the people mule iL almost inevitable ?
These men saw that the oppressions and pro-
fligacy of the rich offered no other chance of
escape to the stuferiog people. Did not the
rule of the late EMPEROR, BO demoralizing, so
tyrannical, so utterly at variance with the
morality and duty of life, lead inevitably to
the conclusion that, sooner or later, a scanda-
lous break-down must take place? Surely we
need not be told that all that followed the
disgraceful war into which that miserable
coxcomb dragged the nation, must have been
maddening to any people situated as the
French were.

The easiest possible way of getting rid of
the difficulty such a state of things presents is
to blame the people—to raise the cries " They
can't be governed," "They are never satisfied."
May it not be more truly slid that the want of
France is men capable of governing. The
llotauoNs wore a miserable break-down.
Intervening Governments between th it and
their setting up ag tin by a conspiracy of
European Sovereigns were the results of
acei.lent and the creatures of violence. LOUIS
PHILIPPE was an offence to all men but those
who trusted for their political salvation to the
till, and the prosperity of the shop. The
Republic has never Wen anything but a brief
breathing spuce used by the factions as oppor-
tunity for intrigue. M. TTTruns said the other
day, alluding to the Rival Princes, that there
were too many of them fur one throne.
Hence, no deubt, they disgust, embroil, and
destroy the nation. If one of them could be
chosen and the rest sunk to the bottom of the
Atlantic, some god might come of sueh an
operation. Or if. in the interior of .kfrioa, Dr.
LIVINCHTONE could tied them thrones, sceptres,
and sooty subjects who some fine morning
would rise hungry and eat them, it would be
a decided benefit to the world. M least it
would be the removal of one great dittiouly for
France.

In the meantime M. 'NIERS seems to find it
very difficult to govern, notwithstanding
the people, as such, are throwing no difficulty
in his way. So far he has only succeeded in

articles.title: ONE QUESTION REFERRED TO THE
articles.text:
ONE QUESTION REFERRED TO THE

POLLING-BOOTH.

Tin session has nearly passed away without
a realisation of the prospect that the Contagious
Diseases Prevention business would be dealt
with accohling to the unquestioned feeling of
the general public. The petitions presented
on Monitay to the Rouse of Commons seem to
have been relied updn- as practical aniswers to
every 'objection: Mr. MARE*, it is true, '
was charged -With petitions from Edinburgh
and other places nuinerously signed; and
praying for the total and unconditional repeal
of Acts which they justly denounced as adapted
to sap the very foundations of society. But
we were alluding to those counter-petitions
which Mr. ETICYN and Sir Jonx PAKINGTON
presented as from the "unfortunates" of
Windsor, Shorncliffe, the Curragli, Ports-
mouth, and Chatham. These women are the
chief petitioners to Parliament for the per-
petuation of the statutes in question. Let us
put the best construction upon their petitions of
which they are susceptible. Be it assumed,
then, that all or many of them have gone into
hospital ' in compliance with the Acts,
and. have thereby recovered the soundness
of body which they had lost. Have
they ceased to be "unfortunates ?" Upon
discharge, did they abandon their former
coarse of life, or did they, in the expressive
language of a sacred writer, return like dogs
to their vomit, and. like sows that had been
viola to their wallowing in the mire? Rad

they acted upon the former alternative, the
medical and military upholders of the sta-
tutes, there is reason to believe, would have
been anything but satisfied. But nothing of
the sort is suggested. On the contrary, we
are left to understand that these precious
laws have promoted. the policy which dictated
their institution, by sending back the " unfor-
tunates " to pursue their vicious: occupations
with diminished. injury to the health of the
troops and. other men who have intercourse
with them.

For some purpose or other, the number of
such women by whom the petitions were
signed, is paraded before Parliament and the
public; and we are all invited to contemplate
with complacency, the fact that the one from
Portsmouth received the signatures of no fewer
than 417 of these women, who arc living
under the special protection of the Imperial
Parliament.

These figures from one place afford an
illustration of the wide and comprehensive
public sanction which the Acts are at this
moment giving to systematically promiscuous
intercourse between the sexes, a sin against
GOD, a crime against human nature, an
offence to purity, and a deadly blow. at family
life and orderly society. What genuine
Liberal can help agreeing with Mr. JACOB
Bina= that the existence of such a system
under the auspices of the present Govern- ,
ment ,reflects, though undeservodly, disgrace
upon the principles which its members pro
fess ? The facts which the Member for
Manchester stated concerning the insulting
conduct of the police under the Act towards
women and girls, on whom they cast un-
merited suspicion, are well fitted to excite to
a high pitch the indignation of husbands,
fathers, and brothers ; and by producing this
effect they will help to procure the re-
peal of the whole system. But it is to
what is inherent in that system that the public
displeasure ought to be chiefly and steadily
directed. The design and the effect of the
Acts are, to sanction, promote, and make safe,
a course of sensual gratification which, in so
fur as it is promiscuous and without the
sanction of lawful wedlock, is as flagrant a
violation of the will of GOD who made us and
of the nature which Ho gave us, as any tram-
' gression condemned in Scripture or visited
with the heaviest legal penalties.
Mr. JACOB BBIGILT deserves public thanks
for having tested the feeling of the House
though at so late a period in the session as to
put on record the votes of not more than a
third part of the people's representatives. We
call upon every elector to scrutinise the
division, to note .well for approval the four
and-seventy men who voted with Mr. JACOB
and to mark for another purpose the
one hundred and forty who voted against him.
It is only by causes of this kind that the
majority of men who aspire to seats in Parlia-
ment can be brought and kept under the
salutary check of public opinion.

articles.title: PROSECUTION OF IRISH PRIESTS.
articles.text:
PROSECUTION OF IRISH PRIESTS.

WE are quite sure that every Liberal man
in the country who has any knowledge what-
ever of the political situation of Ireland, will
receive, with profound, regret, the intimation
that Government is about to prosecute the
parties named by Mr. DOWSE on Tuesday night
last for the part taken by them in the late
Galway election. Such a proceeding may be
justified by high-sounding reference to British
liberty and constitutional usage. We knew
how these flourishes are usually brought in
and made useful for the purpose of satisfying
devotees of law and order. Sensible men,
however, compare what took place in Galway
at the late election, with what has taken
place at a thousand elections in England and
Ireland. time out of mind. It was wrong, we
admit, on the part of these Galway priests, and
others who sided. with them to indulge in
intimidation; but it has been done before,
over and over again, and every sensible man
knows that it has been condoned, as often as
done, by acquiescent Parliaments and Govern-
ments, who were themselves partakers in the
wrong doing, and. gainers by the iniquity. If
the Government candidate had won, there
would. have been no inquiry, and, this prose-
cation Would Liot have taken place, though

the offance, as far as freedom of election
is concerned, would have been no less.
Then, again, it is impossible to read Judge
KEOGH'S address without feeling that he acted
like a red-hot partizan; that whilst he came
down with crushing severity on the priests, he
spared the landlords; and complimented them
for their forbearance, though there could be no
doubt that they indulged in intimidation of a
very gross kind. Mr. GLADSTONE'S position
was, it is true, a difficult one. Priestly offen-
ders against the liberty of election on one
side, and a partizan judge on the other. A
more prudent man would most likely have
thrown the judge over, however inconvenient
such a proceeding might be. Mr. GLADSTONE
has chosen the more dangerous alternative,
and he will have to pay a heavy penalty in
loss of popularity for doing so.
We venture to say that for the last fifty
years, fruitful as Ireland has been in political
misfortunes and entanglements, nothing worse
than this has taken place, and we are mis-
taken if it does not prove to be the chief, the
crowning misfortune of the whole series. The
tenants have boon loft open by law to intimi-
dation, and they have hitherto been intimi-
dated with impunity. Now the law is to be
vindicated, because priests wore the offenders
rather than landlords, and vindicated in a
crusade which will stir up the wildest passions
of the crowd, and penetrate to the hearts of
even the most sober as an insult and an injury.
The liberty of the subject it is true must be
vindicated—but a wise Government would
vindicate it by altering the bad laws under
which it has been constantly violated—by
protecting the voeer from priest and landlord
alike, and not by running a legal muck at a
lot of offenders who but followed an evil
example a thousand times set them by those
in authority, or by those who, acting on the
side of authority, committed their offences
with a glaring impunity.
This decision to prosecute is in truth a bad
business. It is a blundering attempt to ad-
minister justice under circumstances which
stamp it with the character of an incongruous
fully—an untimely zeal, which in effect will
exalt the criminal, and bring contempt and
hatred on the law and those who administer
it.

REVIVERS OF BRITISH INDUSTRY.
JOHN BRIGHT'S letter to Mr. J. ROBERTS,
"President of the Association of Revivers of
Britishindustry,"is short without being, to Mr.
ROBERTS at least, sweet. The present moment
was certainly not quite opportune for a man
to show hicnielf whose business it is to revive
what does not need reviving. The industry
of Great Britain never was so prosperous as it
is, but this gentleman and his companions
have got into their queer heads the idea that
they can bring back a departed higher con-
dition of prosperity of which nobody knows
anything. Mr. BRIGHT in replying to Mr.
ROBERTS tells him that he and his friends are
in a state of mental "muddle," and refuses
to reply to his question as to what he means
by free trade, because Mr. ROBERTS Could not
comprehend anything he might write. He
doubts the sanity of Mr. ROBERTS and his
friends, and on the ground that a corre-
spondence with them could do no good
refuses to enter on so profitless a task.
We think, as Mr. ROBERTS dates from
"Scott's-yard, City, London," he must be a
working man, but the gross stupidity of his
question suggests the idea that he is a dealer
in some small article affected by the French
Treaty, and who thinks the world is going to
fall out of its place in the planetary system
because French lollipops are superseding
British bull's-eyes. There was a great com-
motion of this kind in Bethnal Green during
the late American war amongst the manufac-
turers of "gut." Banjoes had ceased to be
played for a season, as the actual life of the
world was too serious for the nigger melody
' sham; and hence, when bad trade came to the gut
manufacturers, they concluded that free trade
was leading to their ruin, and demonstrated
accordingly. For any working man with any
brains in his head to doubt now the potency
for good of the great principle of free trade
is, no doubt, impossible. If there is anything
in the world which ought to be cast out and left

JULY 27, 1872.

behind, it is the idea of protection as a national
policy. We want, as far as we can possibly gel
it, facility of production and liberty of eit,
change. The tine old country gentlemante
doctrine of protection, by which the people
were plundered and starved, must, we should
think, be .confined to "Scott's-yard" and its
immediate vicinity. The intelligent working
men of England in trades unions and CO
operative societies are not to be taken in by
"Revivers of British Industry," and they
certainly will not blame JOHN BRIGHT for his
scant courtesy to Mr. J. ROBERTS, of" Scott's
-
yard, City, London." Taking the present
industrial condition of the country into
account, and remembering that the hon.
member for Birmingham has been re-
cruiting his health in the solitude of the
hills of Scotland and Wales, it was hardly
to be expected that such a letter as that of
Mr. ROBERTS, the "reviver," could be treated
otherwise than as a very foolish and ill-timed
impertinence.

JULY 27, 1872.

THE MEMOIR TO MR. BRASSEY.

The "Life and Labours of Mr. Brassoy," by
Sir Arthur Helps, K.C.8., has just been issued by
Messrs. Bell and Daldy. It is prefaced by the
following dedication to the Queen :—" To the
Queen. Madam, lam very grateful for the per-
mission given me to dedicate this work to your
Majesty. I desired so to dedicate it, because Ido
not know of any one who has a deeper sympathy
with the labouring-classes than your Majesty, or
any one who takes a more heartfelt interest in
everything that concerns their habits, their edu-
cation, and their general welfare. Moreover, this
sympathy and this interest are not confined to
those classes in your Majesty's dominions only,
but are extended to them wherever they are to be
found. I think also that it cannot but be very
gratifying to your Majesty to have full: evi-
dence that, in a special kind of labour of a very
important character, namely, the construction of
railways, your own subjects have hitherto bornethe
palm, and have introduced their excellent modes
of working into various foreign countries. Your
Majesty will find that the late Mr. Brassey was an
employer of labour after your Majesty's own
heart, always solicitous for the well-being of those
who served under him; never keeping aloof from
them, but using the powerful position of a master
in such a manner as to win their affections and to
diminish the distance which is often far too great
between the employer and the employed. ven-
ture, therefore, to think that the volume will be
interesting to your Majesty on its own account;
and that you will be disposed to view with favour
the merits, if any, and to deal' gently with the
faults of a work written by one who, with all
respect, is ever your Majesty's faithful and devoted
subject and servant, ARTILITII HELPS."

articles.title: WORKING MEN'S CLUBS.
articles.text:
WORKING MEN'S CLUBS.

On Saturday the subjects connected with
the establishment and operations of Working
Men's Clubs were discussed in a conference of
delegates from different London and country
clubs at the South Kensington Museum, Sir
Harcourt Johnstone, M.P., presiding. There
we're present, Mr. HOdgson Pratt, Mr. Alsager
H. Hill, the Rev. 11. Sully, and, in addition to the
representatives of London clubs, delegates from
Northampton, Chelmsford, Bartley in York-
shire, Leighton Buzzard, Bedford, Croydon,
Stratford, and other places, A series of ten
questions was set before the meeting for dis-
cussion, but so much time was spent over two
or three that, while many could only be
touched upon, others had to go without any
oonsideration whatever. The conference was
called by the Working Men's Club and Insti-
tute Union, a central body, which has materially
assisted the formation of the chief clubs
throughout the kingdom, and the chairman,
in opening the proceedings, dwelt upon the
excellent purposes of that Union in assisting
working men to establish and maintain clubs,
which would be to them clubs and institutes,
where they could meet for recreation, refresh-
ment, social intercourse, and self-improvement.
The establishment of clubs was important as
lessening the dependence of the working
classes upon the public-house for refreshment,
recreation, and social intercourse, and for
accommodation for friendly societies' meetings.
The Union had an important work before it,
for it undertook to afford aid and advice to all
who desired to carry on a club; it supplied
the clubs, from the Union's library, with the
best works in the English language ; it lent
the materials for amusing and instructive
lectures, it assisted in obtaining teachers,
lecturers, and readers; it published papers
suggestive of undertakings which might be
carried on in the clubs for the educational
and social advancement of the working
classes, and, by., forming a centre of commu-
nication between different classes, it brought
together men of different social positions, and
thus tended to promote arbitration and con-
ciliation in disputes. He spoke of the large
amounts of money squandered by working
men in public-houses as enormous in the
aggregate, and he urge i that an association
like the "Working Men's Club and Institute
Union," whose purposes, if carried out, would
effhot a great reform in this direction, deserved
the support of all classes. •
The discussion on the questions then arose,
the first being in regard to the best means of
interchanging club membership between the
various clubs affiliated to the parent institution,
and the second the subject of establishing a
building fund for the ereotion of workmen's
clubs. These two questions occupied a long
time and at length they
,were referred the
Council ef the " Union, A long discussion
arose as to the means which should be adopted
to make clubs self-supporting, and several
delegates candidly admitted that when clubs
were established with a programme of tea and
coffee, ginger beer, and such like refreshments,
and newspapers and books for the only reorea-
tion, the clubs soon "foil through ;" but where
beer was sold, and amusements, such as
bagatelle and billiard boards, provided, with
smoking rooms, not only were the expenses
incurred in purchasing the boards soon paid
for but a profit was made. Some temperance
delegates stated that they knew of clubs vilaoh
were self-supporting without the sale of beer,
and. it was retorted that in these cases there
were lists of honorary members, persons who paid
larger subscriptions than the club subscription.
One working man said that the formation of the
clubs would materially lessen the difficulties
connected with the "licensing" and "sale of
liquor" questions, for they would take the
working man from the publichouse, and, by
placing him in a circle where over-drinking
was altogether reprobated, would do vastly
more good to the cause of temperance in a
Month than all the teetotal agitation and Acts
of the Legislature would do in a year. As a
body the teetotallers did not come into the
clubs, and they placed an obstacle between
themselves and the working classes by declar-
ing that the men who were moderate drinkers
were worse than drunkards. It was desirable
that those flubs which had been made self-
supporting should lay before the Council
statements of their mode of working.
Another question then discussed was as to
the measure which should be taken to induce
friendly and trade societies to hold their
meetings (now held in publichouses) in the
clubs. It was declared that these societies
could not meet in the clubs, because no drink
or intoxicating liquors could be sold to non-
members, and the working men members of
these societies were represented as unable to
bear the fatigues of meeting over " friendly "
or trade niatters without having stioh an
amount of intoxicating liquor as would. pay
the publican for lending his room. One
delegate pointed out that it was more profit-
able tor those societies to meet at clubs, and
for the members of them to become club
members, than to go to publichouses, as in the
clubs the best unadulterated beer was sold at
a third less than the price paid at the public- •
house, and even on one glass of beer a day

the member of the club saved all the cost of
his subscription (Bd. a month) and more
besides. The subject of the relation of the
Excise officers towards the clubs then arose,
and Mr. Hodgson Pratt stated that the
" Union " had seen with satisfaction the
Prosecution of a sham club, and he described
how a prosecution against a bona Ale club at
Vauxhall had failed. He read a letter from
ti:e Chancellor of the Exchequer, stating that
clubs desiring to be left unmolested by the
Excise must deposit their rules with the
Board of Inland Revenue (and Mr. Pratt
explained their bye-laws as well), and must
maintain I hose rules. It was shown that the
Board of Inland Revenue had not recognized
this mode of dealing, but it was said that
there was little doubt of the fact that those
clubs which sold liquors for the benefit of the
club itself, and not for the benefit of an in-
dividual, would not be molested.

In the afternoon the delegates visited the
Exhibition, and in the evening had tea,
together in Spiers and Pond's pavilion. In
the evening the annual meeting of the parent
soeiety was held in the Albert Hall. Mr.
Mundella, M.P., presided, and there were
present Lord Lyttelton, the Hon. W. Cowper-
Temple, M.P., and Mr. A. Johnston, M.P.
Letter's in excuse of absence were read from
the Marquis of Lorne, Mr. J. Morley, M.P.,
Sir Stafford Northeote, M.P., and others. The
annual report presented stated that the club
movement was extending itself not only
throughout the kingdom, but to America,
France, Belgium, and other parts of the Con-
tinent. Daring the year 66 new clubs had
started, and 35 had affiliated themselves to
the Union. On the m@tion of Mr. T. Hughes,
M.P., the report was adopted, and Lord
Lyttelton was re-elected president. The
meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks.

articles.title: GREY COAT HOSPITAL, WEST-
articles.text:
GREY COAT HOSPITAL, WEST-

MINSTEU.

A meeting of working men, convened by the
Westminster Working Men's Liberal Associa-
tion, was held on Wednesday evening at Bass's
Assembly Rooms, Pimlico, to consider the
Endowed Schools Commissioners' Scheme for
the above schools. Mr. B. Luoraft, member
of the London School Board, occupied the
chair, and there was a large attendance.

The Chairman, in opening the proceedings,
said that he had found out that a Bill
was laying on the table of • both Houses
of Parliament, which would, on the
4th of August transfer the Grey Coat HoSpital
from the poor of Westminster to tho
"Endowed School Commissioners," finless
something could be done to prevent it, which
he earnestly hoped would be done. He found
from a book published in 1810, on "London
Public Charities,': the following account of the
formation and regulations of Grey Coat School:
In the year 1698 a charity-school was erected in
Tothill-fields, in• the parish of St: Margaret,
Westminster, for the education of poor children,
by the name of the "Grey-Coat :School," from the
colour of the children's uniform. The trustees
whereof by charitable benefactions being greatly
encouraged to proceed, in 1701 not only consider-
ably increased their number of children, but like-
wise plentifully supplied them with all the
necessaries of life, in a large and commodious
building near Tothill-fields wherein, besides their
being taught and instructed in the principles of
religion they are employed in Spinning, km, to
inure them early to industry; and having attained
the necessary qualifications at school they are put
out apprentices. For the encouragement of this
undertaking, Queen Ann, on the 10th of April,
1706, by her letters-patent, incorporated the
trustees by the name of "The Governors of the
Grey-Coat Hospital in Tothill-iields, of the Royal
Foundation of Queen Anne ;" by which name it
has perpetual succession, may sue and be sued,
elect governors in the room of these deceased, and
receive and purchase leads, tenements, &c. in
morttutin, to the yearly amount of 2,000 clear
of reprises; and do all other acts "relating to the
corporation.
This school in the year 1727 wag in so flourish-
ing a state that it contained eighty boys and fifty
girls, in which year the charge of all its disburge-
ments amounted to £1,457 7s. 6d.

In September, 1739, a Mathematical school was
erected upon this foundation, and a proper master
retained to instruct the boys in navigation, and
to fit them for the sea-service; several of them
have since done honour to their profession, and
have become captains in the navy.

There are at this time in the school ninety poor
children, who are not only clothed and instructed,
but maintained in lodging, washing, and board;
they are taught reading, writiug, and arithmetic,
and are carefully educated in the principles of the
Christian religion,according to the Church of Eng-
land. They are publicly examined upon the ex-
position of the dumb. Catechism or Liturgy every
Sunday evening at seven o'clock,

Since the foundation in 1098 the number of
children who have been bound apprentices from
this school amounts to one thousand four hundred
and ninety-eight. The charge of each child is
'computed at £lB 18s. per annum, including
salaries and wages of master, mistress, servants
and the expenses of the infirmary, so that the'
yearly expenditure l these respects amounts to
4i,700. In addition to the endowment, the
finances are assisted by contributions at sermons,
and voluntary benefactions and legacies.
The meeting was then addressed by Mews.

Hearn, Ruby, MoSweeny, Davis, Saddler,
Morton, find others.

The -following resolution and petition was
passed unanimously:--

Resolved,—That in the opinion of this meting;
the scheme now before Parliament for the suPprei-
sion of the "Grey Coat Hospital," an institution
established nearly 200 years, for educating, main.
taining, and apprenticing the children of 'he poor
in the city of Westminsier, is an act of spoliation,
and Might to be resisted.

TO TIIE HONOURABLE VIE COMMONS OF GREAT
BRITAIN .AND IRELAND IN PARLIAMENT ASSEM-
BLED.

The humble petition of inhabitants of the city
of Westminster in public meeting assembled,
Sheweth,—That for nearly two centuries there
has been established in the city of Westminster ati
institution known as the "Grey Coat Hospital,"
educating, maintaining, and apprenticing the
sons and daughters of the poor. Your petitioners
beg permission to state to your Honourable House,
that with great surprise it has come to their know-
ledgethat ascheme is before your Honourable House,
proposing the complete suppression of this institu-
tion, and for your sanction of an expenditure of
£17,000 out of the capital funds of the trust, for
building day and boarding schools.
The fees to which are to be fixed at a rate far
beyond the means of the poor to whora we consider
the endowment belongs.
Your petitioners, therefore,consider it a duty they
owe your Honourable House, to state plainly, but
respectfully, that it appears to them a scheme to
deprive the poor for the benefit of the rich.
Your petitioners pray your Honourable louse
not to sanction this scheme in the present session
so that the working classes may have an oppor-
tunity of considering it during the recess, for the
following reasons :—First ; that it Las come upon
us by surprise. Secondly; that as your petitioners
now view the scheme, it appears a most cruel act
of spoliation. _ _

And your petitioners, as in duty bound, will
ever pray.

Mr, George Potter moved that a deputation
be appointed from the meeting to wait upon
Mr. Gladstone to ask him to postpone the Bill
until next session, in order to give time for the
working classes of -Westminster to express
their opinion upon it.
The motion was carried by acclamation, and
a large deputation appointed.

articles.text:
THE LONDON BAKEHOUSES.

On Saturday night last an open air " indigna-
tion meeting" of journeymen bakers was held in
Bertnondsey-square, Southwark, for the purpose
of protesting aoinst the injustice of the Smoke
Nuisance Act being applied to bakehouses. About
3,000 journeymen were present, who came in
procession, with bands, from a'l parts of London,
and who evinced a lively interest in the proceed-
ings. Mr. E. Adams, a Journeyman, took the
chair, supported by a strong committee, composed
of the officers of the various bakers' societies.
The chairman said the Legislature hail turned a
deaf ear to their well-founded complaints, owing
to the prsjudiced and one-sided statements made
by the Rome Secretary, who seemed obstinately
bent upon punishing the baking trade f-ir reasons
best known to himself. The S.noke Nuisance
Act was a useful Act applied to its legitimate
purposes—to large manufacturing establishments,
with huge chimneys, belching forth volumes of
black, thick smoke at all hours of the day and
night—but to apply such an Act to a small baker's
oven was a monstrous folly and injustice. Under
this Act, both twisters and journeymen bakers
were being continually summoned and fined for
allowing a few puffs of smoke to escape for about
five minutes from their chimneys while lighting
the oven fire. This smoke could not be prevented.
The following resolutions were carried by
acclamation :

1. That this meeting, while deeply sympa-
thizing with their employ era in the injustice
With which they are treated by the Smoke Nuis-
aince Ail, views with great apprehensions the
unwarrantable extension of its provisions to the
operatives, who have neither the ability to comply
with the law, nor the means to pay the heavy
pen dties inflicted.

2. That this meeting, fully conscious of It 4
inability to comply with the law, must indignantly
protest an Act which commits men to prison as
telons unless the unjust tines are paid by their
employers.

3. That the baking trades, having appealed to
the Legislature in vain for exemption trum this
law, the operatives, valuing their liberty at a
higher price than the low wages they receive,
hereby giv the public notice, tut should these
s
persecutions againir their brethren eolitinue, they
will tat" einsnyiel w.tl their employers to cease
manufauturing bread until relief is afforded
them.

4. That this meeting, having no confidence in
Mr. Bruce, the Home Secretary, appoint a deputa-
tion el' 12 journeymen to wait upon Mr. Gladstone,
to lay before him the case of the journeymen, and
acquaint hint with the above resolutions.

With regard to the impending strike among the
London and North-Western Railway Servants, the
answer to the memorial requesting the removal of

Five neglectful parents have been before the
Thames Police Court, at the instance of the

want of clothes as the causes of non-attend-
anee, and they were granted remands, in the

rebuff at Westminster Polite-eourt fur being
unable to substantiate a charge they brought
against two men of having broken the windows
of their chapel and disturbed their worship.
One of their own witnesses testified that they
had got hold of the wrong offender, and the
magistrate dismissed their summonses, with
10s. costs.

To the Editor of the BEE-Hm.

Sin,—On behalf of myself and others, I

notice in your paper of our grievances. You
or the public do not know how we are treated

would say, I only wonder how flesh and blood
can put up with it. Well, Sir, the great secret
is, we, as a body, are not united. Why?
Because of the artful system of promotion,
which is no better than a premium held out to
cut one another's throats; but I do hope that
now men will become more united, and work
together to ()Inuit' the desired objeet —more
wage. I should like to bring before the
public through the medium of your paper, the
so-culled fair way promotions are made, espe-
cially by the surveyor of the metropolitan
district—Mr. Stow. Ido not believe it would
be tolerated for one moment by Parliament.
We are told that we must all pass through
the different grades before reaching the top,
but the present system adopted by the stir
veyor is to place the lowest man at the top
without ever passing through any of the
grades butween the lowest and highest. We
have petitioned, but without effect, and I
believe the only course open to us is through
the medium of the public press. I therefere
trust you will help us through your widely
circulated paper. Apologising for troubling
you with this long letter,—l remain, yours
respectfully,
ONE OF THE MINORS OF THE POST-OFFICE.

THE CURRENCY, STRIKES, &o.
To the Editor of the BEE-RivE.

SIR,—We have advocates enough of Govern-
mental paper issues—we have the whole
country passive under the infliction of a
Receipt Tax. When, however, it is proposed
in a rectified form to unite these two familiar
usages, and so, in the far future, to effect
peaceably certain real reforms in society, none
are found to record their approval—none even
to utter a word in reasonable exposition of the
error—if error it be—of such a proposition.
Among the fruits of such a union would be
the saving of the entire present cost of tax
collection in the country, i.e., about live
millions annually.
Another live millions annually would be
saved by the direct application of such public
paper issue to all imotediate r moval of the
debts of the country, whether national or social.
Further, year by year, other equally large
amounts of public indebtedness would, through
the renewal of issues, be cancelled in a similar
way. Collaterally also, counties, and even
townships on a similar principle could, with
similar results, deal with the local iudehtedikees
of the people,

Thus eventually the now ice-bound
energies of the people would in all directions
be entirely freed from the myriad yokes
capital at present imposes On them, all sources
of income independent of hoour, either of
hand or head, being ultimAtely thus, as they
ought to be,. publicly assumed, and no invest-
ment for eapttul being left but at a moderate
rate of interest, as is quite right also, the

public funds of the country, national or
municipal.
Working men, however, Gould manage all
those things for themselves. When, therefore,
they strike, let them strike not temporarily.
as mere dogs squabbling for a few crumbs more
or less that fall from their masters' table, but
as men, at once and for ever, at every oppor_
tunity, against every selfish proprietor who-
being offered fair terms of union and mutual
Interest, has refused them, and, so far as he is
soneerned, will have nothing but the "devil's
ystem " to the end of time.

In the spice allotted me I cannot express
my full meaning, hut in even what I have
said I cannot, to those who have read any •
thing or remember anything of my former
letters to you, be either vague or obscure.—l
am, Sir, yours, Sm., W. A. RUSSELL.
Greenwich.

VIE WEEK'S NEWS.

The order issued that all eosterm ongers'
stands "or barrows should be cleared away
from the thoroughfares of the New Cut, Lam-
beth Marsh,: by half-past ten on Sunday
morning, was enforced last Sunday by the
officers of the Lambeth vestry. Although there
was a considerable amount of discontent and
grumbling, the costermongers, With some few
exceptions, showed themselves willing to obey
the authorities, but in many instances dis-
persed themselves over the neighbourhood,
where they continued crying their wares. A
large crowd assembled later in the forenoon in
in front of d shop kept by a tradesman who it
was said has been foremost in advocating the
Tradesman's Sunday Closing 'Movement, but
whose shop was open, business being in full
swing. Much hooting and groaning took place,
until the proprietor of the shop thought it
would be better to put his shutters up, and
after a short interval the disturbance sub-
aided.

His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales
visited Trentham, the seat of the Duke of
SUthorland on Monday for the purpose of
taking part in the rejoicings consequent on the
coming of age of the Marquis of Stafford. Earl
Granville was also a guest.

Some confusion attended the first employ-
ment of the ballot, mado at a municipal elec-
tion in Boston a few clays since. Voting-papers
were Oven in folded, and placed in an open
box, instead of being placed under lock and
seal, as the new Act prescribes.

At the inquest at Twickenham on Miss
Hough, who died on Friday from the effects of
a sting by a hee, evidence was given that
death arose from the nervous shock, and that
once before a similar incident had caused her
to be insensible for two hours. The verdict
ascribed death to "Syncope, accelerated by her
having been stung by a

A shocking tragedy has been enacted at
Celina, Mercer county, Ohio. Three men,
named respeetively Jacob Kimmel, .Absolom
Kimmel, and Alexander WLeod, were confined
in gaol on the charge of having outraged and
then murdered a young lady as she was re-
turning from the Sunday school. On the Bth
, inst., three thousand people collected round
the prison, and breaking in took the keys
from the gaoler, brought the three prisoners
out, placed them in a waggon and took them
to the spot where the girl was murdered, and
in sight of the home of the Kimmels. A rude
„gallows was here erected, and halters fixed
round the necks of the prisoners. At this
juneture Elias Seem., brother of the deceased
girl, came forward and pleaded for the life of
Jacob Kimmel, the younger of the criminals,
a lad seventeen years of age, and the crowd.
egreed to this. Absolom.Kimmel then reitera-
ted a confession he had made, and he and
M‘Leod were hanged, the younger Kirnrnel
being taken back to the gaol in order that he
• may be tried.. The father of the Kimmels has
been ordered to leave the country in a speci-
fied time.

It is reported that there is not the slightest
foundation for the statement circulated that,
in the event of a general election, Mr. John
Bright will not again seek the suffrages of the
electors of Birmingham. Writing a few days
ago to one of, his constituents, Mr. Bright said
his state of health is still very uncertain.
Some days he feels as well as ever; while on
others he suffers much from pain lathe head,
and at present ands it necessary to avoid all
undue excitement.

Mr: Frederick Fredericks, his wife, and three
other persons have been summoned before the
Brentford magistrates for performing stage
plays in a booth not duly licensed. In de-
fence, Mr. Fredericks stated that similar sum-
monses against him had been dismissed by Mr.
Patterson and by the Ilford Bench. He said
that it was a case of police persecution, as
they had fetched him a distance of forty miles
to answer the summons. Inspector Tarling,
of the Brentford police, said that, after the
decision of Mr. Patterson, be had received
instructions to follow Mr. Fredericks, and
summon him wherever he could be found.
The Benoit, however, declined to convict, and
the inspector then asked for a case for the
osuperior condo, which was granted.

John Tfolion& Edward Cairns, and William
Rart, being found upon the roof of the Phil-
harmonic Theatre by a policeman, who, heariog
noibe, climbed upon an adjacent wall, and
overlooked them, attempted to explain to Mr.
Hannay, at ClerkPnwell Police court, that the v
merely mounted the roof to conceal thenat a yes

all to the liou,se of Correction for.
